strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: controlling the timing and variables involved in multivariate sequence generation. CLEF offers a simple, modular architecture with an interpretable per-variable scaling mechanism.

The reported forecasting improvements are substantial in several settings. For example, Table 2 shows immediate-prediction MAE AUSPC improving from 27.06 to 10.99 on eICU and from 40.87 to 21.35 on MIMIC-IV for the Transformer backbone.

The experimental scope includes two substantial patient datasets, simulated cellular trajectories, three encoder families, FFN ablations, and 20 SPECTRA splits. Evaluating beyond random patient splits is a useful strength.
weaknesses: The central causal claims are unsupported. Patient conditions are diagnosis codes rather than administered treatments, while cellular conditions are inferred retrospectively from observed state transitions. WOT-CF generates alternative futures by independent resampling, without a controlled intervention on the stated condition. Reconstruction accuracy on these datasets establishes conditional forecasting performance, but does not validate intervention effects or individual causal counterfactuals. No identification assumptions or treatment-confounding analysis bridge this gap.

The formulation does not establish the promised temporal and structural control. Definition 3.1 uses the same time index for condition occurrence and outcome prediction, without separating intervention onset from response time. Preserving the input history follows from forecasting future values; it does not establish causal consistency. There is no explicit invariance mechanism or targeted evaluation showing that intervention-unaffected variables remain unchanged.

The multiplicative decoder has an important unaddressed mathematical limitation. Under Equation 2, any variable whose latest value is zero must remain zero in the prediction, regardless of the condition. The corresponding temporal-concept ratio is also undefined at zero. This is particularly relevant to sparse, log-normalized gene-expression measurements, yet handling of zeros and near-zero values is unspecified.

Novelty and comparative evidence are insufficiently isolated. The main mechanism is a learned multiplicative forecast relative to the latest observation; comparisons against additive residual heads and equally conditioned direct-horizon predictors are missing. SimpleLinear is effectively persistence, and it outperforms CLEF on delayed WOT forecasting. Persistence is nevertheless omitted from the WOT-CF comparison. Exploding VAR errors, reaching approximately 10^39, further weaken the baseline evidence. Condition-removal and time-conditioning ablations are also needed.

The zero-shot interpretation is overstated. WOT-CF places original trajectories in training or validation and their alternative continuations in testing, explicitly sharing their prefixes. The protocol does not establish that test conditions are unseen during training. It therefore supports a narrower claim about alternative continuations of familiar histories, rather than generalization to unseen interventions.

The clinical case studies do not validate actionable interventions. Manually lowering predicted glucose and observing greater similarity to non-diabetic controls is partly built into the edit; associated WBC changes lack interventional ground truth and comparison with an unedited model rollout. Cohort construction also identifies ICD-9 category 250 as equivalent to type 1 diabetes, although that category includes multiple diabetes types. Additionally, Figures 7 and 14 label ratios as observed/CLEF while showing values below one for claimed reductions, leaving the direction of the reported effects ambiguous.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete. The manuscript omits essential details about missing laboratory values, feature scaling, context and forecast-horizon sampling, training duration, and the number of repeated runs underlying error bars. The supplied PDF references a GitHub repository without providing a usable URL. These omissions hinder verification of the substantial reported gains.

The evaluation is substantial, covering biological, clinical, and sales data, synthetic counterfactual benchmarks, distribution-shift experiments, and architectural ablations. Multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, hyperparameters, and computational comparisons strengthen the empirical contribution.
weaknesses: Novelty and attribution remain insufficiently established. The central mechanism predicts per-variable multipliers applied to the latest observation. Comparisons against additive residual prediction, learned linear models, and strong direct horizon-conditioned predictors are needed to distinguish the proposed 'temporal concepts' from a useful persistence-based inductive bias. Appendix A.3's suggestion that long-horizon forecasting necessarily requires autoregression is incorrect.

The advertised control properties exceed what the architecture establishes. Equation 3 does not enforce a multiplier of one for unaffected variables, and Table 5 measures prediction error rather than demonstrating preservation under intervention. The multiplicative decoder also cannot predict a nonzero value when the corresponding latest observation is zero, a consequential restriction for gene expression and sales. Appendix F acknowledges this limitation but does not evaluate a remedy.

The automatic balancing argument is technically unsupported. Separately encoding history and treatment does not make history representations statistically independent of treatment assignment. Assumption 3.4 largely assumes the desired conditional-mean estimation property. Furthermore, Tables 10–12 only examine models with balancing losses, so they do not substantiate the prominent claim that CLEF learns balanced representations without such losses. Higher classifier BCE alone also does not establish treatment invariance.

WOT-CF does not provide intervention-grounded counterfactual truth. Appendix C.1 constructs alternative futures by sampling from the same optimal-transport process, while condition labels are inferred retrospectively from source and destination expression. These are alternative observational trajectories rather than outcomes generated by a specified intervention mechanism. The split also does not establish generalization to held-out conditions, weakening the interpretation of 'zero-shot counterfactual generation.'

The clinical conclusions substantially exceed the evidence. Real-world condition tokens are diagnosis codes rather than administered treatments. Manually changing glucose or WBC multipliers and obtaining greater similarity to non-diabetic patients does not identify an effective clinical intervention or validate its downstream causal effects. The case studies need comparison against otherwise identical, unedited model rollouts and independent intervention evidence.

There are concrete problems in the clinical case-study specification and interpretation. Appendix C.2.3 treats ICD-9 category 250 as equivalent to type 1 diabetes, although that category includes other diabetes types. Figures 7b and 18 label their ratios as observed/CLEF yet interpret values below one as decreases; as labeled, these imply higher generated values. Both issues require resolution before the clinical findings can be trusted.

Comparative performance is mixed despite the broad state-of-the-art framing. SimpleLinear and VAR outperform the neural models on delayed WOT, while Table 8 shows CLEF-xLSTM worsening delayed MAE on both eICU and MIMIC-IV. The forecasting improvements are valuable, but they do not compensate for the unresolved novelty, control, and causal-validity issues at a top-tier acceptance threshold.
